F O U N D AT I O N S
Why coding standards matter
A coding standard is a shared set of rules for how code is written — so any engineer on the team can read, extend, and trust it.
Consistency
Code reads as if written by
one author — no context-
switching. e.g. every file
uses the same brace and
naming style.
Reliability
Rules steer teams from
error-prone constructs. e.g.
banning if (a = b) catches
assign-vs-compare typos.
Maintainability
Future readers spend less
time deciphering intent. e.g.
a clear getTemperature()
needs no comment.
Onboarding
New engineers become
productive sooner. e.g. a
new hire ships a safe fix in
week one.
C O R E Q UA L I T I E S
Readability & maintainability
Readable code
Meaningful names — elapsedTimeMs, not d
Small functions — one job, e.g. parseHeader()
Consistent layout and indentation
Comments explain the "why", not the "what"
No clever tricks that hide behaviour
Maintainable code
Low coupling, high cohesion between modules
One responsibility per unit; easy to test
No magic numbers — e.g. MAX_RETRIES, not 5
Localized change: edits stay contained
Guard rails — const and uint8_t, not raw int
STA N DARDS I N P R ACT ICE
Naming conventions
Principles
Descriptive over short — names should reveal purpose
Consistent case: camelCase, snake_case — pick one
Constants in UPPER_CASE; types clearly marked
Encode units where it matters (…Ms, …Bytes)
Avoid ambiguous abbreviations and single letters
// Avoid
int d; // elapsed what?
float t; // temp? time?
void calc(); // calc what?
// Prefer
uint32_t elapsedTimeMs;
float temperatureC;
void calculateChecksum(void);
STA N DARDS I N P R ACT ICE
Formatting rules
Indentation
Fixed width (e.g. 4 spaces). Never mix
tabs and spaces.
Braces
Always brace blocks — even single
statements — to prevent slips.
Line length
Keep ~80–120 chars so diffs and
reviews stay side-by-side.
One per line
One statement and one declaration per
line for clean diffs.
Spacing
Consistent blank lines and operator
spacing aid scanning.
Automate it
Let a formatter enforce style so reviews
focus on logic.
R E L I A B I L I T Y
Safe programming practices
Defensive habits that keep embedded and industrial code predictable under real-world conditions.
Initialize everything
Every variable set before use — never
rely on undefined state. e.g. uint8_t crc
= 0U;
Check return values
Handle every error code and status; fail
safe, not silent. e.g. if (fclose(f) != 0) {
handle }
Bound your accesses
Guard loops and array indices to
prevent overruns. e.g. if (i < LEN) buf[i] =
x;
Fixed-width types
Prefer uint32_t over int for portable,
predictable sizes.
Limit dynamic memory
Avoid heap allocation on safety-critical
paths. e.g. use a static pool[], not
malloc().
Explicit conversions
No implicit casts — make every
conversion intentional. e.g. y =
(uint16_t)x;
S E C T I O N 0 4
Introduction to MISRA
Motor Industry Software Reliability Association
A widely adopted set of guidelines for writing safe, portable, and reliable C and C++ —used across automotive, medical,
aerospace, and industrial systems.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
How the guidelines are organized
Directives vs. Rules
Directives
Guidance where compliance needs more than source
code — process, design intent, and documentation.
Rules
Requirements checkable directly from source code —
often enforced automatically by tools.
Mandatory
Must always comply — no deviations permitted. e.g. never use an
object after its lifetime ends.
Required
Comply, or record a formal, justified deviation. e.g. deviate from
single-exit only with sign-off.
Advisory
Recommended; deviations tracked, lighter weight. e.g. prefer one
return per function.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
In practice: do & don't
DON'T
if (x = getStatus()) { … }
// assignment inside condition
for (i = 0; i < 10; i++)
// magic number, plain int
p = malloc(n);
// heap on critical path
DO
status = getStatus();
if (status != 0) { … }
for (i = 0U; i < MAX_ITEMS; i++)
// named bound, unsigned
static Item pool[MAX_ITEMS];
// static allocation
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Assignments hidden in conditions, magic numbers, and heap on the hot path cause the silent, hard-to-reproduce failures that dominate
embedded defects.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: variables & values
DON'T
// Rule 9.1 — set before use
uint8_t crc; crc ^= b;
// Rule 14.4 — Boolean condition
if (len) { ... }
// Rule 7.1 — no octal constants
mode = 052;
DO
// Rule 9.1 — set before use
uint8_t crc = 0U; crc ^= b;
// Rule 14.4 — Boolean condition
if (len != 0U) { ... }
// Rule 7.1 — no octal constants
mode = 42;
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Uninitialised reads, accidental octal literals, and non-boolean conditions are classic undefined-behaviour bugs the compiler won't flag for you.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: types & conversions
DON'T
// Rule 7.2 — suffix unsigned constants
x = 40000;
// Rule 10.4 — no mixed-sign arithmetic
if (u32 > s32) { ... }
// Rule 11.3 — no pointer-type casts
p32 = (uint32_t *)pByte;
DO
// Rule 7.2 — suffix unsigned constants
x = 40000U;
// Rule 10.4 — no mixed-sign arithmetic
if (u32 > (uint32_t)s32) { ... }
// Rule 11.3 — no pointer-type casts
(void)memcpy(&v, pByte, sizeof v);
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Explicit types and suffixes keep arithmetic and pointers behaving identically across every compiler and target, instead of silently truncating data.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Essential types: keep categories clean
DON'T
// Rule 10.1 - bool used in arithmetic
total = isReady + count;
// Rule 10.3 - narrowing assignment
uint8_t b = 300;
// Rule 10.4 - mixed signedness
if (u32 + s32 > 0U)
DO
// Rule 10.1 - keep bool in boolean use
total = count + (isReady ? 1 : 0);
// Rule 10.3 - value fits the type
uint8_t b = 200U;
// Rule 10.4 - same essential type
if (u32 + (uint32_t)s32 > 0U)
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Keeping essential-type categories consistent stops the implicit conversions that silently change a value or its signedness between platforms.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: comments & types
DON'T
// Rule 3.1 — no nested comments
/* start /* nested */
// Rule 8.2 — name every parameter
int add(int, int);
// Dir 4.6 — use fixed-width typedefs
int len;
DO
// Rule 3.1 — no nested comments
/* start - nested */
// Rule 8.2 — name every parameter
int add(int a, int b);
// Dir 4.6 — use fixed-width typedefs
uint16_t len;
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Non-nested comments, named parameters, and fixed-width types remove ambiguity for both the reader and the compiler across different
platforms.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: expressions & switch
DON'T
// Rule 12.1 — make precedence explicit
r = a || b && c;
// Rule 16.3 — end every case with break
case 1: f(); case 2: g(); break;
// Rule 13.3 — no side effects with ++
a[i] = i++;
DO
// Rule 12.1 — make precedence explicit
r = a || (b && c);
// Rule 16.3 — end every case with break
case 1: f(); break; case 2: g(); break;
// Rule 13.3 — no side effects with ++
a[i] = i; i++;
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Clear precedence, no hidden side effects, and a break on every case stop the fall-through and evaluation-order surprises that are easy to miss in
review.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: control flow & functions
DON'T
// Rule 15.6 — always brace
if (ok) doWork();
// Rule 16.4 — switch needs default
switch (s) { case 1: f(); break; }
// Rule 17.7 — use return values
getStatus();
DO
// Rule 15.6 — always brace
if (ok) { doWork(); }
// Rule 16.4 — switch needs default
switch (s) { case 1: f(); break;
default: /* none */ break; }
// Rule 17.7 — use return values
status = getStatus();
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Braces, a default case, and checked return values close the gaps where a one-line edit or an ignored error code quietly becomes a field failure.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: loops & recursion
DON'T
// Rule 14.1 — no float loop counter
for (float f = 0; f < 1; f += 0.1f)
// Rule 14.2 — keep for loops well-formed
for (i = 0; i < n; i++, n--)
// Rule 17.2 — no recursion
int f(int n){ return f(n-1); }
DO
// Rule 14.1 — no float loop counter
for (uint8_t i = 0U; i < 10U; i++)
// Rule 14.2 — keep for loops well-formed
for (i = 0U; i < n; i++)
// Rule 17.2 — no recursion
use an explicit loop or stack
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Well-formed loops and no recursion guarantee bounded execution time and stack use, vital where a runaway loop or deep call chain can crash a
real-time system.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: scope & declarations
DON'T
// Rule 8.9 — scope to one function
static int count; // file scope
// Rule 5.3 — no name shadowing
int x; { int x = 0; }
// Rule 17.4 — return on every path
if (a) { return 1; }
DO
// Rule 8.9 — scope to one function
void f(void) { int count; }
// Rule 5.3 — no name shadowing
int x; { int xInner = 0; }
// Rule 17.4 — return on every path
if (a) { return 1; } return 0;
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Narrow scope, no shadowed names, and a return on every path make functions easier to reason about and remove whole classes of undefined
behaviour.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: macros & pointers
DON'T
// Rule 20.7 — parenthesize macro args
#define SQ(x) x * x
// Rule 11.8 — cast strips const, write corrupts
data
const char *cp = msg;
char *p = (char *)cp;
// Rule 18.4 — no pointer arithmetic
p = p + 2;
DO
// Rule 20.7 — parenthesize macro args
#define SQ(x) ((x) * (x))
// Rule 11.8 — keep const, compiler blocks writes
const char *cp = msg;
const char *p = cp;
// Rule 18.4 — no pointer arithmetic
p = &arr[2];
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Fully parenthesised macros, preserved const and volatile, and array indexing over pointer maths keep low-level code predictable and safe to
refactor.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: arrays & bounds
DON'T
// Rule 18.1 — stay within the array
p = &arr[0]; q = p + 20;
// Rule 18.8 — no variable-length arrays
int buf[n]; // n is a variable
// Dir 4.11 — check library arguments
y = sqrt(x);
DO
// Rule 18.1 — stay within the array
if (i < LEN) { v = arr[i]; }
// Rule 18.8 — no variable-length arrays
int buf[MAX_LEN];
// Dir 4.11 — check library arguments
if (x >= 0.0) { y = sqrt(x); }
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Staying inside array bounds and avoiding variable-length arrays prevents the buffer overruns and unpredictable stack growth behind many safety
faults.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Basic rules: the preprocessor
DON'T
// Rule 20.4 — no keyword macro names
#define int long
// Rule 20.10 — # stringizes, obscures intent
#define LOG(x) log_msg(#x)
LOG(state);
// Rule 21.1 — no reserved identifiers
#define _MAX 10
DO
// Rule 20.4 — no keyword macro names
typedef long wide_t;
// Rule 20.10 — write the string directly
log_msg("state");
// Rule 21.1 — no reserved identifiers
#define APP_MAX 10
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Disciplined preprocessor use and avoiding reserved names keep code portable and readable, so what you see is what the compiler actually
builds.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Banned standard-library functions
DON'T
// Rule 21.3 - no malloc/free
p = malloc(n);
// Rule 21.7 - no atoi/atof
v = atoi(str);
// Rule 21.8 - no system()
system("reboot");
DO
// Rule 21.3 - static allocation
static Item pool[MAX_ITEMS];
// Rule 21.7 - use strtol()
v = strtol(str, &end, 10);
// Rule 21.8 - call a safe API
platform_reset();
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Avoiding dynamic memory, weak string conversions, and process-control calls removes non-deterministic standard-library behaviour embedded
code can't tolerate.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
Directives: defensive design
DON'T
// Dir 4.1 — minimize run-time failures
y = a / b;
// Dir 4.7 — test returned error info
(void)readSensor();
// Dir 4.12 — no dynamic memory
buf = malloc(len);
DO
// Dir 4.1 — minimize run-time failures
if (b != 0) { y = a / b; }
// Dir 4.7 — test returned error info
if (readSensor() != OK) { ... }
// Dir 4.12 — no dynamic memory
static uint8_t buf[MAX_LEN];
W H Y I T MAT T E R S
Handling every error, documenting run-time checks, and banning dynamic memory keep behaviour deterministic, the core requirement for
certifiable software.
M I S R A G U I D ELI NE S
A compliance mindset
Compliance is a mindset, not a checkbox — understand the intent behind each rule, and handle exceptions openly.
01
Understand intent
Each rule exists to remove a
real risk — learn the "why".
e.g. no-recursion guards
against stack overflow.
02
Document deviations
When a rule can't be met,
record rationale, risk, and
approval. e.g. log rule,
reason, risk, approver.
03
Keep a compliance record
Track guideline status
across the codebase. e.g. a
matrix of rule → status →
owner.
04
Tools plus people
Automate what you can;
judge the rest. e.g. the linter
flags it, a reviewer approves
the exception.

Peer review
Prepare ›Review ›Discuss ›Rework ›Approve
Reviewers focus on
Correctness and edge cases
Standard & MISRA compliance
Readability and clear naming
Adequate tests for the change
Habits of good reviews
Keep changesets small and focused
Critique the code, not the author
Be specific, kind, and actionable
Use a shared review checklist
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Static analysis concepts
Static analysis examines code without executing it — finding defects the compiler and tests may miss.
Finds hidden risks
Undefined behaviour, null
derefs, uninitialized
variables, dead code.
Enforces MISRA
Flags guideline violations
automatically as code is
written. e.g. warns on if (a =
b) as you type it.
Runs in CI
Gate every merge; treat new
warnings as build-breaking
errors.
Baseline & burn down
Record existing findings,
then drive the count to zero.
e.g. 400 today → 0 over the
quarter.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Static analysis: tools & metrics
Teams run one or more analyzers in CI, and track a few key measures to see quality trends over time.
Commercial analyzers
Polyspace, Coverity
Klocwork, Helix QAC
LDRA, Parasoft C/C++test
PC-lint Plus, Astrée
Open-source analyzers
Cppcheck
Clang Static Analyzer
clang-tidy
SonarQube
Complexity measures
Cyclomatic complexity
Nesting depth
Function length (LOC)
Comment density
Quality measures
Rule / MISRA violations
Defect density
Code duplication %
Maintainability index
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Which parameters matter —and why
Each measure flags a specific risk in the code. Here is what the analyzer looks at, a concrete example, and why it matters.
Parameter
What the analyzer checks (example)
Why it matters
Cyclomatic complexity
A routine with layered if / else and a switch has ~15
independent paths.
Needs ~15 tests for full coverage and is hard to
verify
— cap around 10 per function.
Nesting depth
An if inside a for inside a while inside an if
— four-
plus levels deep.
Deeply nested logic is hard to read and test; flatten
with guard clauses (keep ≤ 4).
Rule / MISRA violation
Ignoring malloc()’s return value, or an implicit signed
/ unsigned conversion.
Can trigger undefined behaviour or crashes; must
be fixed or formally justified.
Code duplication
The same 30
-line validation block copied across
three modules.
Every fix must be repeated in each copy
— raises
defect risk; keep under ~5%.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: wrong data type, flagged —and fixed
The analyzer flags a plain int used where an exact width and sign are required — the behaviour then depends on the target platform.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
// 32-bit hardware register
int reg;
reg = read_register();
if (reg > 0x7FFFFFFF) {
handle_overflow();
}
#include <stdint.h>
// 32-bit hardware register
uint32_t reg;
reg = read_register();
if (reg > 0x7FFFFFFFu) {
handle_overflow();
}
Warning — Plain int has platform-dependent width and sign; the comparison can
overflow or never hold (MISRA Dir 4.6).
✓ Fixed — A fixed-width uint32_t makes size and sign explicit, so the code behaves the
same on every target.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: commented-out code, flagged —and fixed
Static analyzers flag commented-out code as dead code — it drifts out of date, misleads readers, and belongs in version control.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
int total(int a, int b) {
// int old = a * b;
// return old - tax(a);
return a + b;
}
int total(int a, int b) {
return a + b;
}
// History lives in version
// control, not in comments.
Warning — Commented-out code is dead code — it goes stale and confuses readers
(MISRA advisory Rule 2.4).
✓ Fixed — Delete the dead lines and rely on version control for history, keeping the function
easy to read.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: uninitialized variable, flagged —and fixed
The analyzer flags a variable that is read before it is assigned — its starting value is indeterminate, so the result is undefined.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
int sum_array(const int *a, int n) {
int sum;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
sum += a[i];
return sum;
}
int sum_array(const int *a, int n) {
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
sum += a[i];
return sum;
}
Warning — sum is read before it is initialized — its starting value is indeterminate (CWE-
457 / MISRA Rule 9.1).
✓ Fixed — Initialize sum to 0 at its declaration so the accumulation starts from a known
value.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: magic numbers, flagged —and fixed
Unnamed literals scattered through the code hide intent and are easy to change inconsistently. Give each one a descriptive name.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
if (temp > 85) {
shutdown();
}
delay(85); // a different 85
#define MAX_TEMP_C 85
#define COOLDOWN_MS 85
if (temp > MAX_TEMP_C) {
shutdown();
}
delay(COOLDOWN_MS);
Warning — The literal 85 appears unnamed with two unrelated meanings — unclear
intent and risky to change.
✓ Fixed — Named constants document intent and let each value change independently
and safely.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: unchecked malloc(), flagged —and fixed
A MISRA / CWE rule violation the analyzer catches in CI: the return value of malloc() is used before it is checked for NULL.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
void load_config(void) {
char *buf = malloc(256);
read_file(buf, 256);
parse(buf);
free(buf);
}
// buf may be NULL here
void load_config(void) {
char *buf = malloc(256);
if (buf == NULL) {
return; // on failure
}
read_file(buf, 256);
parse(buf);
free(buf);
Warning — malloc() return value used without a NULL check (MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.12 /
CWE-690). ✓ Fixed — Allocation failure is handled before use, so the pointer is guaranteed valid.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: high cyclomatic complexity, flagged —and fixed
Every branch adds an independent path the analyzer counts. A long if / else chain pushes complexity up; a lookup table collapses it.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
int price(int tier) {
if (tier == 1) return 10;
else if (tier == 2) return 20;
else if (tier == 3) return 30;
else if (tier == 4) return 40;
else if (tier == 5) return 50;
else return 0;
}
static const int TABLE[] =
{ 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 };
int price(int tier) {
if (tier < 1 || tier > 5)
return 0;
return TABLE[tier];
}
Warning — Complexity grows with every branch — many paths to test and easy to get
wrong (target ≤ 10).
✓ Fixed — One table lookup replaces six branches — a single path that is easy to test and
extend.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: deep nesting, flagged —and fixed
Logic nested four-plus levels deep is hard to read and every branch needs coverage. Guard clauses flatten it to a single level.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
int save(Item *it) {
if (it != NULL) {
if (it->valid) {
if (it->size > 0) {
return write(it);
}
}
}
return -1;
}
int save(Item *it) {
if (it == NULL) return -1;
if (!it->valid) return -1;
if (it->size <= 0) return -1;
return write(it);
}
Warning — Nesting depth of 4 — arrow-shaped code that is hard to read and fully test. ✓ Fixed — Guard clauses return early, keeping the body at depth 1 — linear and easy to
follow.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: duplicated logic, flagged —and fixed
The analyzer detects the same validation copied in two functions — a fix in one copy can be missed in the other. Extract it once.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
void add_user(User u) {
if (u.name == NULL || u.age < 0)
return;
insert(u);
}
void edit_user(User u) {
if (u.name == NULL || u.age < 0)
return;
update(u);
}
static bool valid(User u) {
return u.name && u.age >= 0;
}
void add_user(User u) {
if (valid(u)) insert(u);
}
void edit_user(User u) {
if (valid(u)) update(u);
}
Warning — The same validation is duplicated across functions — a change must be
made in every copy. ✓ Fixed — A single shared check — update it once and both call sites stay correct.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: buffer overflow, flagged —and fixed
The analyzer flags an unbounded copy into a fixed-size buffer — input longer than the buffer overruns adjacent memory.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
char name[16];
strcpy(name, input);
printf("Hi %s", name);
// input may exceed 16 bytes
char name[16];
snprintf(name, sizeof(name),
"%s", input);
printf("Hi %s", name);
Warning — strcpy() has no bound; a long input overruns name[16] and corrupts memory
(CWE-120 / MISRA Rule 21.17).
✓ Fixed — snprintf() with sizeof(name) truncates safely, so the copy can never exceed the
buffer.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: resource leak, flagged —and fixed
The analyzer flags a file handle that is not closed on every path — an early return leaks the resource each time it runs.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
FILE *f = fopen(path, "r");
if (read_header(f) != OK)
return -1;
process(f);
fclose(f);
return 0;
// f leaks on the error path
FILE *f = fopen(path, "r");
if (read_header(f) != OK) {
fclose(f);
return -1;
}
process(f);
fclose(f);
return 0;
Warning — f is not closed on the early-return path — every failure leaks a file handle
(CWE-775).
✓ Fixed — Close f before the error return so the handle is released on every path out of the
function.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: assignment in condition, flagged —and fixed
The analyzer flags = used where == was intended — the condition assigns instead of comparing, and is almost always a bug.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
int rc = do_work();
if (rc = 0) {
// never reached
log_success();
}
handle(rc);
int rc = do_work();
if (rc == 0) {
log_success();
}
handle(rc);
Warning — rc = 0 assigns, then tests 0 (always false) — success is never logged (CWE-
481 / MISRA Rule 13.4). ✓ Fixed — Use == to compare; the branch now runs when do_work() actually returns 0.
C ATC HI NG D E F E CTS E A R LY
Example: missing break in switch, flagged —and fixed
The analyzer flags an unintended fall-through — without break, control drops into the next case and runs extra code.
① FLAGGED BY ANALYZER ② CORRECTED
switch (mode) {
case READ:
open_input();
case WRITE:
open_output();
break;
}
switch (mode) {
case READ:
open_input();
break;
case WRITE:
open_output();
break;
}
Warning — READ falls through into WRITE, so open_output() runs unintentionally (CWE-
484 / MISRA Rule 16.3). ✓ Fixed — Add break after each case so only the matching branch executes.

C A S E ST U DY
A defect caught before release
Illustrative example — representative of a typical embedded defect
BUFFER OVERRUN → BOUNDED COPY
// Bug: off-by-one overruns buf
uint8_t buf[64];
for (i = 0; i <= len; i++)
buf[i] = rx[i]; // writes buf[64]
// Fix: bound + unsigned counter
if (len > sizeof(buf)) return ERR;
for (i = 0U; i < len; i++)
buf[i] = rx[i];
Symptom
Intermittent watchdog resets under heavy message traffic.
Root cause
An off-by-one loop wrote one byte past a 64-byte buffer.
Caught by
Static analysis flagged the boundary; peer review confirmed
it.
Lesson
Bound every access; unsigned counters and size checks stop
overruns.

Quality is built in, not bolted on
Standards make code consistent, readable, and safe to change.
MISRA and safe practices reduce risk in embedded & industrial systems.

A P P E N D IX
Glossary & references
Glossary
MISRA — Guidelines for safe, portable C/C++ in critical systems.
Static analysis — Inspecting source code for defects without running
it.
Cyclomatic complexity — Count of independent paths through a
function.
Deviation — A documented, approved exception to a guideline.
Coverage — Share of code exercised by the test suite.
Coupling / cohesion — Dependence between modules / focus within
one module.
